nameStory: The name 'peanut' is a bit misleading since these aren't actually nuts at all – they're legumes, like peas and beans! The 'pea' part of the name hints at their true family relationships, while 'nut' refers to their hard shell and nutty flavor. Some folks call them 'groundnuts' or 'goobers,' which better reflects their unique habit of burying their developing pods underground.
description: The peanut is a low-growing, bushy annual plant that reaches about 1-2 feet tall and spreads outward. It has compound leaves with four oval leaflets arranged in pairs, and produces small yellow flowers that look typical of the pea family. After pollination, the flowers develop a remarkable trick – they actually push their developing seed pods underground to mature, making this one of nature's most unusual gardening stories.

idTips.label: Underground Fruiting
idTips.description: The plant's most unique feature – after yellow flowers are pollinated, they develop pointed structures called 'pegs' that grow downward and push the developing pods 1-3 inches into the soil where they mature

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small bright yellow flowers about half an inch across with the typical pea-family shape – a banner petal on top, two wing petals on sides, and a boat-shaped bottom petal

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves with exactly four oval leaflets arranged in two pairs, each leaflet about 1-2 inches long with a smooth, slightly waxy feel and prominent veining

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low, spreading bushy plant that grows outward more than upward, with multiple branching stems that feel somewhat succulent and have tiny hairs when examined closely

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: The familiar peanuts develop inside wrinkled, beige pods underground – each pod typically contains 1-4 seeds with papery reddish-brown skins that rub off easily

habitat: In New England, peanuts are extremely rare and found only in cultivated gardens or experimental plots, as our climate is too cool and our growing season too short for reliable production. When grown here, they need the warmest, most protected spots with well-draining, loose soil that allows their developing pods to penetrate easily underground.

seasonality.spring: Seeds are planted after all danger of frost has passed, typically late May to early June in New England, when soil temperatures reach at least 65°F consistently.
seasonality.summer: Plants grow rapidly in hot weather, producing their characteristic yellow flowers from July through August, followed by the fascinating underground pod development process.
seasonality.fall: Plants begin yellowing and dying back with the first light frosts, signaling that any underground pods should be harvested before hard freezes damage them.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground presence – this tropical annual cannot survive New England winters, though harvested peanuts store well indoors.

funFact: Peanut plants literally plant their own seeds – after the flowers are pollinated, they grow a pointed spike called a 'peg' that acts like a tiny drill, boring into the soil where the peanut pod develops in complete darkness underground, making them one of the only crops that farms itself!
confusionNotes: The four-leaflet arrangement might be confused with some clovers, but peanut leaflets are much larger and arranged in two distinct pairs rather than radiating from a central point. The yellow pea-family flowers and unique underground fruiting behavior are dead giveaways once you know what to look for.
contextualKnowledge: Despite the name, peanuts are not nuts at all but legumes closely related to peas and beans, which is why people with tree nut allergies can often eat peanuts safely (though peanut allergies are a separate, serious concern). This naming confusion has led to decades of dietary mix-ups and explains why peanut butter is sometimes called 'groundnut butter' in other countries.
compareHints: Peanuts are the only species in their genus (Arachis) that you'll encounter in New England, but they can be compared to other legume family members like garden peas and beans. Unlike those climbing or upright relatives, peanuts stay low and bushy, and most remarkably, they're the only common legume that buries its developing seeds underground rather than holding them up in the air.
